questions.q: Which two mechanisms allow the kidney to produce concentrated urine?
questions.explain: The loop of Henle builds the gradient. The vasa recta preserve it.

open.q: Which two mechanisms allow the kidney to produce concentrated urine?

questions.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent multiplier?
questions.explain: The loop multiplies a small horizontal gradient into a large vertical one.

open.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent multiplier?

questions.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent exchanger?
questions.explain: Blood flows in a hairpin, taking up water from the medulla without washing out its solutes.

open.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent exchanger?

questions.q: What is the maximum osmolality the human kidney can reach in urine?
questions.explain: It is limited by the medullary gradient. Plasma is about 300 mOsm/L.

open.q: What is the maximum osmolality the human kidney can reach in urine?

questions.q: What is the main transport feature of the thick ascending limb?
options: It is impermeable to water and actively reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺ and 2Cl⁻
It is highly permeable to water
It reabsorbs water under ADH control
questions.explain: NKCC2 pumps solutes out while water stays in, so the fluid becomes dilute. This is the diluting segment.

open.q: What is the main transport feature of the thick ascending limb?

questions.q: Is the tubular fluid entering the distal convoluted tubule hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic compared with plasma?
questions.explain: The thick ascending limb removes solute without water, leaving the fluid at about 100 mOsm/L.

open.q: Is the tubular fluid entering the distal convoluted tubule hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic compared with plasma?

questions.q: Which solutes mainly create the high osmolality of the renal medulla?
questions.explain: NaCl is pumped out of the ascending limb. Urea is recycled from the collecting duct.

open.q: Which solutes mainly create the high osmolality of the renal medulla?

questions.q: Which hormone makes the collecting duct permeable to water so that urine can be concentrated?
questions.explain: Without ADH, the collecting duct stays water-impermeable and dilute urine is passed.

open.q: Which hormone makes the collecting duct permeable to water so that urine can be concentrated?

options: Lack of kidney response to ADH
questions.explain: Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary reduces ADH. It responds to desmopressin.

options: Failure of ADH synthesis in the hypothalamus
Failure of the collecting duct to respond to ADH
questions.explain: ADH levels are normal or high, but the kidney does not respond. Desmopressin does not help.

questions.q: What urine is typical of diabetes insipidus?
options: Large volumes of urine with glucose
questions.explain: The patient has polyuria and polydipsia, with low urine osmolality and no glycosuria.

open.q: What urine is typical of diabetes insipidus?

questions.q: Which diuretic impairs the countercurrent multiplier by blocking the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter?
questions.explain: Loop diuretics abolish the medullary gradient, so urine cannot be concentrated.

open.q: Which diuretic impairs the countercurrent multiplier by blocking the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter?

questions.q: What is the lowest urine osmolality the kidney can produce (maximally dilute urine)?
questions.explain: With no ADH, the kidney can excrete urine at about 50 mOsm/L.

open.q: What is the lowest urine osmolality the kidney can produce (maximally dilute urine)?
